parsed_answer.content:
In the Java I/O architecture, the distinction between Byte Streams and Character Streams is fundamental to how the JVM handles data encoding and binary integrity. Byte Streams, rooted in the abstract classes InputStream and OutputStream, operate on raw 8-bit bytes. They are agnostic to the content, making them the appropriate choice for binary data like images, serialized objects, or encrypted payloads. They do not perform any character encoding translation, which preserves the exact bit-for-bit structure of the source.

Character Streams, rooted in Reader and Writer, were introduced to handle 16-bit Unicode characters. When you read from a Character Stream, the JVM performs an implicit transformation: it reads raw bytes from the underlying source and decodes them into Java's internal UTF-16 char format based on the platform's default charset or a specified Charset object. This abstraction is essential for text processing, as it abstracts away the complexity of multi-byte character encodings like UTF-8 or ISO-8859-1, preventing common bugs where partial multi-byte sequences are misread as invalid characters.

items: Byte Streams are the foundation of all I/O; Character Streams are actually decorators that wrap Byte Streams, using the StreamDecoder/StreamEncoder classes to bridge the gap between raw bytes and Unicode characters.

Character Streams maintain an internal buffer to handle multi-byte characters efficiently. If a character spans multiple bytes, the Reader keeps the state until the full sequence is decoded, preventing data corruption.

The 'default' charset used by Character Streams is determined by the 'file.encoding' system property, which can lead to non-deterministic behavior across different OS environments if not explicitly defined in your code.
Using a Byte Stream to read text files often leads to 'mojibake' or encoding errors, especially when dealing with non-ASCII characters that occupy multiple bytes.

parsed_answer.content: Senior Engineer Insight: Never rely on the platform default charset. Always pass a StandardCharsets constant to your Readers and Writers. A common production nightmare occurs when a service running on a Linux container (defaulting to UTF-8) reads a file generated by a legacy Windows system (defaulting to Windows-1252), resulting in corrupted logs or malformed configuration data. Always be explicit.

title: What is byte stream versus character stream?
